Living Timeline • Part 1: Magic Bullets, Blood Groups & Early Antibiotics (1900–1940)

Instructions: Complete the timeline sketches and notes as you master each enquiry lesson.
1901 • Karl Landsteiner: ABO Blood Groups Discovered Key Topic 4.1

Landsteiner identifies A, B, and O blood groups, proving agglutination occurs when incompatible blood types mix. This discovery transforms blood transfusions from fatal gambles into safe, predictable surgical lifelines, foundational for modern trauma surgery.

1909 • Paul Ehrlich & Sahachiro Hata: Salvarsan 606 Key Topic 4.1

Building on dye research, Ehrlich and Hata systematically test hundreds of arsenic compounds, discovering arsphenamine (compound 606). Humanity’s first synthetic chemical ‘magic bullet’ targets syphilis bacteria without poisoning human tissue.

1928 • Alexander Fleming: Accidental Discovery of Penicillin Key Topic 4.2

Returning from holiday, Fleming notices a contaminated staphylococcus culture dish with a halo of destroyed bacteria around Penicillium notatum mould. Fleming publishes in 1929, though unable to purify or extract enough active substance for clinical trials.

1932 • Gerhard Domagk: Prontosil & Sulfonamide Drugs Key Topic 4.1

Domagk demonstrates that the red leather dye Prontosil cures streptococcal blood poisoning in mice (and saves his own daughter’s arm). Chemists isolate the active ingredient sulfonamide, launching the world’s first mass-prescribed class of antibacterial wonder drugs.

2/24 The 20th century transformed pharmacology from toxic general poisons into targeted magic bullets.

Living Timeline • Part 2: Mass Antibiotics, The NHS, DNA & Oncology (1940–present)

Instructions: Complete the timeline sketches and notes as you master each enquiry lesson.
1941–44 • Florey, Chain & Heatley: Penicillin Mass Production Key Topic 4.2

Howard Florey and Ernst Chain purify penicillin at Oxford, successfully treating mice and Albert Alexander (1941). Heatley and Florey travel to Peoria, Illinois, using corn-steep liquor and deep-tank fermentation to produce 2.3 million doses for D-Day casualties.

1948 • Aneurin Bevan: Foundation of the NHS Key Topic 4.3

On 5 July 1948, the National Health Service opens at Park Hospital, Manchester. Championed by Bevan and the 1942 Beveridge Report, it nationalises voluntary and municipal hospitals, providing universal healthcare free at the point of clinical delivery.

1953 • Watson, Crick & Franklin: DNA Double Helix Structure Key Topic 4.4

Using Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins’s X-ray crystallography (Photograph 51), Watson and Crick deduce the double-helix structure of DNA at Cambridge, unlocking hereditary genetic code and modern molecular gene therapy.

1971–2003 • CT Scanners (1971) & The Human Genome Project (2003) Key Topic 4.4 • 4.5

Godfrey Hounsfield invents the EMI CT scanner, combining computer algorithms with X-rays to image internal organs without surgery. In 2003, the international Human Genome Project maps all 3 billion chemical base pairs in human DNA, founding precision medicine.

3/24 From the birth of the NHS to the sequencing of the human genome, state action and high-tech science transformed health.
KEY TOPIC 4.1 • ENQUIRY LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL PAPER 1 (1HI0/11) • THEMATIC STUDY

Why did the discovery of DNA revolutionize understanding of disease causes, yet take decades to yield treatments?

Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take precise, structured notes alongside each milestone as your teacher narrates the history
1 c1900–1940s
Mendel & Early Genetics
• Mendel’s pea plant laws rediscovered
• Chromosomes observed in cell nuclei
• Garrod links genes to metabolism
• Proteins wrongly assumed to carry code
Focus Clue
Why did doctors assume proteins carried hereditary traits?
2 1951–1952
Franklin & Photograph 51
• Rosalind Franklin at King’s College
• Expert in X-ray crystallography
• May 1952: Captures Photograph 51
• X-shaped diffraction proves double helix
Focus Clue
How did Photograph 51 prove DNA’s helical structure?
3 1953
Watson & Crick’s Model
• Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge
• Wilkins shares Franklin’s data
• March 1953: 3D wire & metal model built
• Base pairing: A-T and C-G replication
Focus Clue
How did base pairing explain hereditary replication?
4 1990–2003
Human Genome Project
• International public consortium (1990)
• Mapped all 3 billion base pairs in DNA
• Identified 20,000–25,000 human genes
• Completed 2003: genetic blueprint open
Focus Clue
Why was mapping 3 billion base pairs a medical milestone?
5 2000s–Present
Screening & Treatment Gap
• Screening faulty genes (BRCA1/2, CF)
• Tailored targeted pharmacogenomics
• Treatment gap: cause known, cure hard
• CRISPR gene editing ethical debates
Focus Clue
Why did understanding causes outpace finding cures?
4/24 Franklin’s 62-hour X-ray exposure revealed the double helix; Watson and Crick celebrated in The Eagle pub.

KEY TOPIC 4.2 • ENQUIRY LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL PAPER 1 (1HI0/11) • THEMATIC STUDY

Were high-tech diagnostic scanners more vital to modern health than state lifestyle campaigns?

Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take precise, structured notes alongside each milestone as your teacher narrates the history
1 1895–1918
Röntgen & Early X-Rays
• Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays (1895)
• Passes through tissue; dense bones show
• Marie Curie runs mobile WWI X-ray cars
• Ended blind probing for bullets in war
Focus Clue
How did X-rays transform surgical trauma diagnosis in WWI?
2 1930s–1960s
Blood Labs & Endoscopy
• Automated blood labs track chemistry
• Cellular staining detects abnormalities
• Harold Hopkins invents fiber endoscope
• Visual inspection of gut without surgery
Focus Clue
Why was fiber-optic endoscopy superior to exploratory surgery?
3 1971–1980s
Hounsfield’s CT & MRI
• Godfrey Hounsfield invents CT scan (1971)
• Rotating X-rays form 3D body slices
• Mansfield & Lauterbur develop MRI
• Radio waves image soft brain tumours
Focus Clue
Why did CT scans transform internal soft-tissue diagnosis?
4 c1950–1980s
Epidemiological Shift
• Antibiotics conquer infectious killers
• Life expectancy rises above 75 years
• Rise of chronic non-communicable disease
• Smoking, diet, and alcohol blamed
Focus Clue
What drove the shift from infectious to lifestyle diseases?
5 1980s–Present
State Lifestyle Campaigns
• Compulsory laws: seatbelts (1983)
• Health Act 2006: 2007 public smoking ban
• Fiscal nudge: 2018 Sugar Tax on drinks
• Education: "5 A Day" & "Change4Life"
Focus Clue
Why do governments favour lifestyle prevention over treatment?
8/24 Bertha Röntgen cried "I have seen my death!" upon seeing her bones; doctors saw the dawn of non-invasive diagnosis.

KEY TOPIC 4.3 • ENQUIRY LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL PAPER 1 (1HI0/11) • THEMATIC STUDY

Was the establishment of the NHS in 1948 more transformative than the development of magic bullets?

Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take precise, structured notes alongside each milestone as your teacher narrates the history
1 1906–1909
Ehrlich & Salvarsan 606
• Paul Ehrlich tests bacterial chemical dyes
• Conceives synthetic "magic bullets"
• Sahachiro Hata joins team (1909)
• Compound 606 cures syphilis in humans
Focus Clue
Why was Salvarsan 606 termed the first "magic bullet"?
2 1932–1935
Domagk & Prontosil
• Gerhard Domagk tests red industrial dye
• 1932: Prontosil kills strep in mice
• Cures daughter’s severe blood poisoning
• Active ingredient: sulfonamide drugs
Focus Clue
How did Prontosil prove synthetic drugs could kill microbes?
3 1942
The Beveridge Report
• Sir William Beveridge social report
• Tackles "Five Giants" including Disease
• Proposes universal state social care
• Wartime collectivism spurs support
Focus Clue
How did WWII unity create momentum for state healthcare?
4 1945–1948
Bevan & Launch of the NHS
• Aneurin Bevan appointed Health Minister
• BMA doctors resist state salaries (90%)
• Bevan lets consultants keep private beds
• 5 July 1948: NHS free at point of care
Focus Clue
How did Bevan compromise to persuade resistant doctors?
5 1950s–Present
High-Tech Care & Costs
• Dialysis, hip replacements & transplants
• Keyhole surgery & chemotherapy units
• 1951 prescription charges divide party
• Aging population strains tax funding
Focus Clue
Why has modern medical success created financial strain?
12/24 Ehrlich tested 605 failed arsenic compounds before compound 606 finally cured syphilis in 1909.

KEY TOPIC 4.4 • ENQUIRY LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL PAPER 1 (1HI0/11) • THEMATIC STUDY

Why did penicillin require a global war and American industrial might to become a mass-produced cure?

Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take precise, structured notes alongside each milestone as your teacher narrates the history
1 1928–1929
Fleming’s Discovery
• St Mary’s Hospital, London (1928)
• Contaminated staphylococcus petri dish
• Penicillium notatum mould dissolves germs
• Publishes 1929; cannot chemically purify
Focus Clue
Why could Fleming not turn mould into a clinical medicine?
2 1938–1940
Florey & Chain at Oxford
• Oxford team reviews Fleming’s paper
• Rockefeller Foundation funds research
• Norman Heatley builds bedpan apparatus
• Freeze-drying extracts pure penicillin
Focus Clue
How did Norman Heatley solve the purification challenge?
3 1940–1941
Mice Trials & Albert Alexander
• May 1940: 4 treated infected mice survive
• 1941: Policeman Albert Alexander treated
• Fatal facial septicaemia clears rapidly
• Drug runs out; patient dies; proof clear
Focus Clue
Why was Alexander’s trial both a success and a tragedy?
4 1941–1944
Peoria & US Mass Production
• Florey & Heatley travel to USA (1941)
• Peoria lab uses corn-steep liquor boost
• Cantaloupe mould strain yields 200x
• 10,000-gallon deep-tank vats built
Focus Clue
How did US industrial fermentation enable mass production?
5 1944–Present
D-Day & Superbugs
• 2.3m doses produced for D-Day (1944)
• Wound fatality drops from 15% to 1%
• Fleming, Florey, Chain win Nobel (1945)
• Overuse drives resistant MRSA superbugs
Focus Clue
Why did Fleming warn that antibiotic overuse causes resistance?
16/24 Fleming almost washed his petri dish in Lysol, but noticed a clear halo where mould destroyed golden staphylococci.

KEY TOPIC 4.5 • ENQUIRY LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL PAPER 1 (1HI0/11) • THEMATIC STUDY

Why has the modern fight against lung cancer required state coercion rather than laboratory cures?

Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take precise, structured notes alongside each milestone as your teacher narrates the history
1 1920s–1950
The Mysterious Epidemic
• British lung cancer deaths surge 15-fold
• Doctors blame tarmac dust or motor fumes
• Tobacco companies market cigarettes
• By 1950: 65% of adult British males smoke
Focus Clue
Why did early doctors fail to link smoking to lung cancer?
2 1950–1954
Doll & Hill’s Proof
• Doll & Hill survey 20 London hospitals
• 1950 BMJ paper links smoking to tumors
• British Doctors Study tracks 40,000 GPs
• Proves heavy smokers face 50x risk
Focus Clue
How did statistical epidemiology prove the causal link?
3 1962–1971
Royal College & Ad Bans
• 1962: Royal College report sounds alarm
• 1965: TV cigarette advertising banned
• 1971: Warning labels on tobacco packets
• Industry sponsors sports to bypass bans
Focus Clue
Why did government action encounter strong tobacco lobbying?
4 2000s
Public Smoking Ban
• Second-hand passive smoke proven toxic
• Health Act 2006: July 2007 indoor ban
• Legal buying age raised from 16 to 18
• UK smoking falls from 65% to under 13%
Focus Clue
Why was passive smoking crucial in banning public smoking?
5 2010s–Present
Plain Packs & Oncology
• 2016: Plain drab-olive packaging law
• Low-dose spiral CT & bronchoscopy
• Robotic VATS lobectomies & immunotherapy
• 16% 5-year survival: prevention vital
Focus Clue
Why does low cancer survival prove prevention beats cure?
20/24 Doll and Hill proved smoking caused lung cancer in 1950; Doll immediately extinguished his pipe and lived to age 92.
